This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.

L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference

sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Codeine, a morphinan opioid sharing the hydromorphone scaffold, had 80.5% oral bioavailability in healthy subjects after oral and IV administration, directly supporting F ≥ 20% for a close structural analogue.
Pentazocine, a benzomorphan opioid with phenol and tertiary amine groups like hydromorphone, showed mean systemic availability of 0.68–0.70 in cirrhotic patients, well above the 20% threshold.
Meptazinol, a phenol-containing analgesic, had absolute bioavailability of 27.9% in cirrhotic patients, above the threshold even with disease-related impairment.
Pethidine, an opioid analgesic, had systemic availability of 0.80 in cirrhotic patients, supporting high oral F for opioids.
Melperone, a basic lipophilic drug, had absolute bioavailability of 54–67% in fasted healthy volunteers, supporting that basic amines with similar properties can exceed 20%.
Rigid lipophilic drugs such as norethisterone (49–80%) and ethinyloestradiol (76.9%) also show high oral bioavailability, consistent with the query's rigid, lipophilic scaffold.
The lowest supplied F values (praziquantel 27.2%, meptazinol 27.9%) remain above 20%, so no affirmative record supports F < 20%.

evidence_gaps: No direct hydromorphone absolute bioavailability record is present in the supplied evidence; prediction relies on structurally related opioids and physicochemical priors.
Most high-F records come from different disease populations (cirrhosis, cystic fibrosis) or different chemical classes, so transferability is inferred rather than measured.
The low neutral fraction (0.1) and possible first-pass metabolism at the phenol/amine are not quantified by direct hydromorphone data.
Some records report systemic availability or unspecified bioavailability type rather than strictly absolute F, though all are above the 20% threshold.
